# Figures with ggplot2

<style>
  :root {
    --footer-text:  "Figures with ggplot2";
    --qr:           `r qr_css`;
    --lecture:      `r lecture_label`;
  }
</style>

::: {.fact}
`Did you know:` snowshoe hares are brown in summer and white in winter. The timing of the two moults is thought to be set mainly by [day length]{.hl}.

_Source: Mills et al. (2013), PNAS_
:::

## Why two lectures on figures

You have made plots with `ggplot2` before, in Statistics (for Linguists) or in the data visualisation workshop. This lecture and the next one go through the basics quickly and spend the time on what makes a figure good enough for a thesis or a paper.

. . .

- Today: the grammar, then control over every part of a plot: colour, shape, legends, scales and themes
- Next time: honest figures, plotting models, and preparing figures for publication

## Today

1. The grammar in five minutes
2. Colour
3. Shape, size and transparency
4. Scales, labels and legends
5. Themes

## The data {.smaller}

A simulated production study: 20 speakers, 10 with English and 10 with Italian as their first language, read 12 words for each of six English vowels. The vowels are named by Wells's lexical sets.

```{r}
set.seed(2028)
speakers <- tibble(speaker = sprintf("S%02d", 1:20),
                   l1 = rep(c("English", "Italian"), each = 10),
                   gender = rep(c("female", "male"), times = 10),
                   scale = if_else(gender == "female", 1.15, 1) * rnorm(20, 1, 0.04))
targets <- tibble(vowel = c("FLEECE", "KIT", "DRESS", "TRAP", "START", "GOOSE"),
                  F1 = c(290, 410, 560, 700, 720, 320),
                  F2 = c(2250, 1950, 1800, 1650, 1150, 1250),
                  dur = c(150, 90, 100, 140, 170, 160))
vowels <- crossing(speakers, targets, token = 1:12) |>
  mutate(F1 = case_when(l1 == "Italian" & vowel == "KIT" ~ 330,
                        l1 == "Italian" & vowel == "TRAP" ~ 620, .default = F1),
         F2 = case_when(l1 == "Italian" & vowel == "KIT" ~ 2150,
                        l1 == "Italian" & vowel == "TRAP" ~ 1720, .default = F2),
         dur = if_else(l1 == "Italian", 125, dur),
         F1 = round(F1 * scale + rnorm(n(), 0, 35)),
         F2 = round(F2 * scale + rnorm(n(), 0, 110)),
         duration = round(dur * rnorm(n(), 1, 0.15)),
         vowel = factor(vowel, levels = targets$vowel)) |>
  select(speaker, l1, gender, vowel, token, F1, F2, duration)
```

## The data

```{r}
vowels
```

. . .

What we built in: the Italian speakers merge KIT with FLEECE, move TRAP toward DRESS, and make all vowels about the same length.

# The grammar in five minutes

::: {.fact}
`Did you know:` Mills and colleagues followed 148 radio-collared snowshoe hares every week for three years. A hare counted as [mismatched]{.hl} when its coat was at least 60 percentage points whiter than the ground around it.

_Source: Mills et al. (2013), PNAS_
:::

## Data, aesthetics, geometry

Every `ggplot2` figure starts from [data]{.hl}, a data frame with one row per observation. The [aesthetics]{.hl}, set inside `aes()`, say which variables go to `x`, `y`, colour or size, and the [geometries]{.hl} say how each row is drawn: as points, lines, bars or boxes.

. . .

[Scales]{.hl}, [facets]{.hl}, [coordinates]{.hl} and a [theme]{.hl} are optional, and each is added with `+`.

## A first plot

```{r, fig.height = 3.0}
ggplot(vowels, aes(x = F2, y = F1)) +
  geom_point()
```

All the data are there, but the axes run the wrong way for a vowel chart.

## A vowel chart

```{r, fig.height = 2.5}
ggplot(vowels, aes(x = F2, y = F1, colour = vowel)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3) +
  scale_x_reverse(position = "top") +
  scale_y_reverse(position = "right")
```

Reversed axes put front vowels on the left and high vowels at the top, as in the IPA chart.

## Layers stack {.smaller}

```{r, fig.height = 2.5}
overall_means <- summarise(vowels, F1 = mean(F1), F2 = mean(F2), .by = vowel)
ggplot(vowels, aes(x = F2, y = F1, colour = vowel)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.15) +
  stat_ellipse(level = 0.68) +
  geom_text(data = overall_means, aes(label = vowel), fontface = "bold", size = 5) +
  scale_x_reverse(position = "top") +
  scale_y_reverse(position = "right") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

Each layer can take its own data. The mappings in `ggplot()` apply to every layer that does not override them.

## Facets {.smaller}

```{r, fig.height = 3.0}
vowel_means <- summarise(vowels, F1 = mean(F1), F2 = mean(F2), .by = c(l1, vowel))
ggplot(vowels, aes(x = F2, y = F1, colour = vowel)) +
  stat_ellipse(level = 0.68, linewidth = 1) +
  geom_text(data = vowel_means, aes(label = vowel), size = 4) +
  scale_x_reverse(position = "top") + scale_y_reverse(position = "right") +
  facet_wrap(~ l1) + theme(legend.position = "none")
```

Small multiples: same axes, one panel per group. KIT and FLEECE overlap in the Italian panel.

## Choosing a geometry

| What you show | Geometry |
|:--|:--|
| One continuous variable | `geom_histogram()`, `geom_density()` |
| A continuous variable by group | `geom_boxplot()`, `geom_violin()`, plus the points |
| Two continuous variables | `geom_point()`, `geom_smooth()` |
| Change over time or along a scale | `geom_line()` |
| Counts of categories | `geom_bar()`, or `geom_col()` for counts you already have |

## Distributions by group {.smaller}

```{r, fig.height = 3.2}
ggplot(vowels, aes(x = vowel, y = duration, fill = l1)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA, alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = l1), size = 0.6, alpha = 0.3,
             position = position_jitterdodge(jitter.width = 0.15, dodge.width = 0.75)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Duration (ms)", fill = NULL, colour = NULL)
```

`position_jitterdodge()` puts the points over the right box. English speakers contrast long and short vowels; Italian speakers do not.

# Colour

::: {.fact}
`Did you know:` in the same Montana study, the hares did not start their moults earlier or later when the snow came late or melted early. Only the [rate]{.hl} of the spring moult changed a little.

_Source: Mills et al. (2013), PNAS_
:::

## Mapping or setting?

```{r, fig.height = 2.3}
p_map <- ggplot(vowel_means, aes(F2, F1)) + geom_point(aes(colour = "blue"), size = 3)
p_set <- ggplot(vowel_means, aes(F2, F1)) + geom_point(colour = "blue", size = 3)
p_map + p_set
```

- Inside `aes()`, `"blue"` is [mapped]{.hl}: it is treated as a variable with one value, which gets the first colour of the scale and a legend
- Outside `aes()`, the colour is [set]{.hl}: every point in the layer is blue

## `colour` or `fill`?

- Points, lines and text have a `colour`
- Areas (bars, boxes, violins, ribbons) have a `fill`, and `colour` is their outline
- Shapes 21 to 25 are points with both: `colour` for the border, `fill` for the inside
- `alpha` sets transparency for both

## Three kinds of palette

```{r palette-kinds, echo = FALSE, fig.height = 3.4}
pals <- bind_rows(
  tibble(type = "Qualitative: categories without an order", col = RColorBrewer::brewer.pal(7, "Dark2")),
  tibble(type = "Sequential: from low to high", col = RColorBrewer::brewer.pal(7, "Blues")),
  tibble(type = "Diverging: below and above a meaningful midpoint", col = RColorBrewer::brewer.pal(7, "RdBu"))
) |>
  mutate(i = rep(1:7, 3), type = fct_inorder(type))
ggplot(pals, aes(i, 0, fill = col)) +
  geom_tile(colour = floor_col, linewidth = 2) +
  scale_fill_identity() +
  facet_wrap(~ type, ncol = 1) +
  theme_void(base_family = plot_font) +
  theme(strip.text = element_text(colour = mist, hjust = 0, size = 15, margin = margin(t = 6, b = 4)))
```

Choose the palette from the type of variable you are showing.

## Your own colours {.smaller}

```{r, fig.height = 3.2}
l1_colours <- c(English = "#E69F00", Italian = "#56B4E9")
ggplot(vowels, aes(x = vowel, y = duration, fill = l1)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA, colour = mist) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = l1_colours) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Duration (ms)", fill = NULL)
```

With a [named vector]{.hl}, colours stay with their categories when a group is dropped or the order changes, and `l1_colours` can be reused in every figure of a paper.

## Palettes for every reader

- Red–green colour-vision deficiencies are common, especially among men: in a lecture hall, assume several readers cannot tell your red from your green
- Figures are also printed in greyscale and shown on dim projectors
- [Okabe–Ito]{.hl}: eight colours that stay distinct for the common deficiencies, built into `R` (4.0 or later)

```{r}
okabe <- unname(palette.colors(palette = "Okabe-Ito"))
okabe
```

## Okabe–Ito in practice {.smaller}

```{r, fig.height = 3.0}
ggplot(vowels, aes(x = F2, y = F1, colour = vowel)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = okabe[2:7]) +
  scale_x_reverse(position = "top") + scale_y_reverse(position = "right") +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(override.aes = list(alpha = 1, size = 4))) +
  theme(legend.position = "right")
```

The first colour is black, which disappears on a dark background. `override.aes` makes the legend keys solid while the points stay transparent.

## Sequential {.smaller}

```{r, fig.height = 2.9}
ggplot(vowels, aes(x = F2, y = F1, colour = duration)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  scale_colour_viridis_c(option = "magma", begin = 0.2) +
  scale_x_reverse(position = "top") + scale_y_reverse(position = "right") +
  facet_wrap(~ l1) +
  labs(colour = "Duration (ms)") + theme(legend.position = "right")
```

[Viridis]{.hl} palettes rise evenly in lightness, so they also work in greyscale. `begin` drops the darkest end, which would vanish on this background.

## Diverging {.smaller}

```{r, fig.height = 2.3}
vowels |>
  summarise(duration = mean(duration), .by = c(speaker, l1, vowel)) |>
  mutate(relative = duration - mean(duration), .by = speaker) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = vowel, y = speaker, fill = relative)) +
  geom_tile() +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#2166AC", mid = "white", high = "#B2182B", midpoint = 0,
                       limits = \(x) c(-1, 1) * max(abs(x))) +
  facet_wrap(~ l1, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Speakers", fill = "ms from the\nspeaker's mean") +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_blank(), panel.grid = element_blank(), legend.position = "right")
```

Diverging palettes suit a meaningful midpoint. [Symmetric limits]{.hl} make equal distances from zero equally dark.

## Highlight instead {.smaller}

```{r, fig.height = 2.9}
focus <- filter(vowels, vowel %in% c("FLEECE", "KIT"))
ggplot(vowels, aes(x = F2, y = F1)) +
  geom_point(colour = vine, alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_point(data = focus, aes(colour = vowel), alpha = 0.5) +
  scale_x_reverse(position = "top") + scale_y_reverse(position = "right") +
  facet_wrap(~ l1) + theme(legend.position = "right")
```

With more than six to eight categories, readers can no longer match colours to labels. [Highlighting]{.hl} colours what the text is about and leaves the rest grey.

# Shape, size and transparency

::: {.fact}
`Did you know:` in a later study of 186 radio-collared hares, those whose coat did not match the ground had up to 7% lower [weekly survival]{.hl}.

_Source: Zimova, Mills & Nowak (2016), Ecology Letters_
:::

## Ranking the channels

```{r channels, echo = FALSE, fig.height = 3.3}
tibble(channel = c("position on a common axis", "length", "angle and slope", "area (size)",
                   "colour lightness", "colour hue"),
       rank = 6:1) |>
  mutate(channel = fct_reorder(channel, rank)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = rank, y = channel)) +
  geom_col(fill = kingfisher, width = 0.65) +
  labs(x = "more accurate for numbers  →", y = NULL) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_blank(), panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
        axis.text.y = element_text(size = 15, colour = mist))
```

Readers compare [positions]{.hl} best and colours worst (after Cleveland & McGill, 1984). Put the comparison that matters on `x` or `y`.

## Redundant coding {.smaller}

```{r, fig.height = 2.8}
speaker_means <- summarise(vowels, F1 = mean(F1), F2 = mean(F2), .by = c(speaker, l1, vowel))
ggplot(speaker_means, aes(x = F2, y = F1, fill = l1, shape = l1)) +
  geom_point(size = 3, colour = floor_col, stroke = 0.6) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(English = 21, Italian = 24)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = l1_colours) +
  scale_x_reverse(position = "top") + scale_y_reverse(position = "right") +
  theme(legend.position = "right")
```

Colour and shape show the same variable ([redundant coding]{.hl}), so the groups survive greyscale printing. Shapes 21–25 take a `fill` and an outline `colour`.

## Transparency and overplotting

```{r, fig.height = 2.8}
p_solid <- ggplot(vowels, aes(F2, F1)) + geom_point(colour = kingfisher)
p_alpha <- ggplot(vowels, aes(F2, F1)) + geom_point(colour = kingfisher, alpha = 0.1)
p_solid + p_alpha
```

With 1,440 solid points, [overplotting]{.hl} hides where the data are dense. With `alpha = 0.1`, the dense regions become darker.

## Size

- Size is read as [area]{.hl}, and readers underestimate differences in area
- Map size only to a continuous variable, never to categories
- `scale_size_area()` makes zero have no size, so area is proportional to the value
- Line width (`linewidth`) and line type can separate a few groups of lines, alongside colour

# Scales, labels and legends

::: {.fact}
`Did you know:` for western Montana, Mills and colleagues projected [29 to 35]{.hl} fewer days of snow cover per year by the middle of this century, and 40 to 69 fewer by its end.

_Source: Mills et al. (2013), PNAS_
:::

## What a scale does

Every aesthetic has a [scale]{.hl}: it turns data values into positions, colours or sizes, and draws the axis or legend that reads them back.

- `scale_<aesthetic>_<type>()`: `scale_x_continuous()`, `scale_colour_manual()`, `scale_fill_viridis_c()`
- `name`, `breaks`, `labels` and `limits` work the same way in all of them
- `labs()` is a shortcut for the names

## Breaks and labels {.smaller}

```{r, fig.height = 3.0}
ggplot(vowels, aes(x = F2, y = F1, colour = vowel)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.2) +
  scale_x_reverse(position = "top", breaks = seq(800, 2800, by = 400),
                  labels = scales::label_comma(suffix = " Hz")) +
  scale_y_reverse(position = "right", breaks = seq(200, 1000, by = 200),
                  labels = scales::label_comma(suffix = " Hz")) +
  labs(x = "F2", y = "F1", colour = NULL)
```

`{scales}` has a labeller for most needs: percentages, thousands separators, units, dates.

## Labels

```{r, eval = FALSE}
labs(title = "Italian speakers merge KIT and FLEECE",
     subtitle = "Mean formants per speaker, 12 tokens per vowel",
     x = "F2 (Hz)", y = "F1 (Hz)", colour = NULL,
     caption = "Simulated data. Ellipses cover 68% of tokens.")
```

- Axis titles written as words with [units]{.hl}, such as "F1 (Hz)" for the variable `F1`
- `colour = NULL` removes a legend title that only repeats what the keys say
- A title that states the finding, and a caption that says what the reader sees

## Legend order {.smaller}

```{r, fig.height = 3.1}
ggplot(vowels, aes(x = duration, colour = fct_reorder(vowel, duration, .desc = TRUE))) +
  geom_density(linewidth = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~ l1) +
  labs(x = "Duration (ms)", y = "Density", colour = NULL) +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(nrow = 1))
```

The legend follows the order of the [factor levels]{.hl}, so to change the legend, reorder the factor.

## Legends: position and keys

```{r, eval = FALSE}
theme(legend.position = "bottom")
theme(legend.position = "inside", legend.position.inside = c(0.85, 0.2))
theme(legend.position = "none")
guides(colour = guide_legend(nrow = 1, override.aes = list(alpha = 1, size = 4)))
guides(fill = "none")
```

- A legend inside an empty corner of the panel saves space
- Two legends for the same variable merge when they have the same title and labels

## Direct labels {.smaller}

```{r, fig.height = 3.2}
ggplot(speaker_means, aes(x = F2, y = F1, colour = vowel)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_text(data = vowel_means, aes(label = vowel), fontface = "bold", size = 5) +
  scale_x_reverse(position = "top") + scale_y_reverse(position = "right") +
  facet_wrap(~ l1) + theme(legend.position = "none")
```

[Direct labels]{.hl} next to the data save the reader from looking back and forth between plot and legend.

# Themes

::: {.fact}
`Did you know:` individual snowshoe hares differ widely in when they moult. That variation is what [natural selection]{.hl} could act on if snow seasons keep getting shorter.

_Source: Zimova, Mills & Nowak (2016), Ecology Letters_
:::

## What a theme controls {.smaller}

Everything that is not data: fonts, background, grid lines, axis ticks, legend layout, facet strips.

| Element | Changed with | Example |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Text | `element_text()` | `axis.title = element_text(size = 12)` |
| Lines | `element_line()` | `panel.grid.major = element_line(colour = "grey90")` |
| Boxes | `element_rect()` | `plot.background = element_rect(fill = "white")` |
| Nothing | `element_blank()` | `panel.grid.minor = element_blank()` |

## A theme of your own {.smaller}

```{r}
theme_paper <- function(base_size = 11, base_family = "") {
  theme_minimal(base_size = base_size, base_family = base_family) +
    theme(plot.background = element_rect(fill = "white", colour = NA),
          panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
          panel.grid.major = element_line(colour = "grey90"),
          axis.title = element_text(colour = "grey30"),
          strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", hjust = 0),
          plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
          plot.title.position = "plot",
          legend.position = "bottom")
}
```

Write the [theme function]{.hl} once, keep it in a file, and `source()` it at the top of every script for the same paper. `theme_set(theme_paper())` makes it the default.

## The theme in use {.smaller}

```{r, fig.height = 3.4}
ggplot(speaker_means, aes(x = F2, y = F1, colour = vowel)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_text(data = vowel_means, aes(label = vowel), fontface = "bold", size = 4.5) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = okabe[2:7]) +
  scale_x_reverse(position = "top") + scale_y_reverse(position = "right") +
  facet_wrap(~ l1) + labs(x = "F2 (Hz)", y = "F1 (Hz)") +
  theme_paper(base_size = 16) + theme(legend.position = "none")
```

## Built-in starting points

Start from the built-in theme closest to what you want, such as `theme_minimal()`, `theme_classic()` or `theme_bw()`, and change the rest with `theme()`. `base_size` scales all text at once, so set it for the size the figure will have on the page (next lecture).

. . .

In `ggplot2` 4.0 or later, built-in themes also take `ink`, `paper` and `accent` colours, for example `theme_minimal(paper = "white", ink = "grey20")`.

## Summary

::: {.takeaway}
- A plot is [data]{.hl}, [aesthetics]{.hl} and [geometries]{.hl}, plus scales, facets and a theme; each layer can take its own data
- Map a variable inside `aes()`; set a fixed value outside it
- Choose a [qualitative]{.hl}, [sequential]{.hl} or [diverging]{.hl} palette from the type of variable, and check it for colour-vision deficiency and greyscale
- Show important comparisons by position; use colour, shape and size for the rest, and code key groups twice
- Scales control breaks, labels and legends; direct labels often beat a legend
- Write a theme function once and use it for every figure in a paper
:::

## References {.refs}

- Cleveland, W. S., & McGill, R. (1984). Graphical perception: Theory, experimentation, and application to the development of graphical methods. _Journal of the American Statistical Association_, 79(387), 531–554.

- Wells, J. C. (1982). _Accents of English_. Cambridge University Press.
- [Wickham, H., Navarro, D., & Pedersen, T. L. (n.d.). _ggplot2: Elegant graphics for data analysis_ (3rd ed., online). https://ggplot2-book.org]{.hl}
- Wilke, C. O. (2019). _Fundamentals of data visualization_. O'Reilly. https://clauswilke.com/dataviz/

- Mills, L. S., Zimova, M., Oyler, J., Running, S., Abatzoglou, J. T., & Lukacs, P. M. (2013). Camouflage mismatch in seasonal coat color due to decreased snow duration. _Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences_, 110(18), 7360–7365. https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1222724110
